 1   Q   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY IN THIS

                    I. BOOK DEPRECIATION CONCEPTS

27   Q   PLEASE EXPLAIN THE PURPOSE OF BOOK DEPRECIATION

28       ACCOUNTING.

29   A   Book depreciation is the recognition in a utility’s income statement of the

30       consumption or use of assets to provide utility service. Book depreciation

                                       Page 3
                                Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews
                                 NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1           is recorded as an expense and is included in the ratemaking formula to

2            calculate the utility’s overall revenue requirement. 1

3                    The basic underlying principle of utility depreciation accounting is

4            intergenerational equity, where the customers and ratepayers who benefit

5            from the generated service of assets pay all the costs for those assets during

6            the benefit period, which is over the life of those assets. This concept of

7            intergenerational equity can be achieved through depreciation by allocating

8            costs to customers in a systematic and rational manner that is consistent with

 9           the period of time in which customers receive the service value of the asset. 2

10                   Book depreciation provides for the recovery of the original cost of

11           the utility’s assets that are currently providing service. Book depreciation

12           expense is not intended to provide for replacement of the current assets, but

13           provides for capital recovery or return of current investment.




             1
               Edison Electric Institute, Introduction to Depreciation for Public Utilities and
     Other Industries, April 2013, page viii.
             2

 1   Q   ARE         THERE        ANY      DEFINITIONS          OF      DEPRECIATION

 2       ACCOUNTING THAT ARE UTILIZED FOR RATEMAKING

 3       PURPOSES?

 4   A   Yes. One of the most quoted definitions of depreciation accounting is the

 5       one contained in the Code of Federal Regulations:

 6              Depreciation, as applied to depreciable electric plant, means the loss
 7              in service value not restored by current maintenance, incurred in
 8              connection with the consumption or prospective retirement of
 9              electric plant in the course of service from causes which are known
10              to be in current operation and against which the utility is not
11              protected by insurance. Among the causes to be given consideration
12              are wear and tear, decay, action of the elements, inadequacy,
13              obsolescence, changes in the art, changes in demand and
14              requirements of public authorities. 3

15              Effectively, depreciation accounting provides for the recovery of the

16       original cost of an asset, adjusted for net salvage, over its useful life.



17   Q   WHY DOES DEPRECIATION DEPEND ON THE USEFUL LIFE OF

18       THE ASSET?

19   A   Generally, capital recovery of an asset occurs over the Average Service Life

20       (“ASL”) of that asset. As a result, it is critical that appropriate average

21       service lives be used to develop the depreciation rates so that no current or

22       future generation of ratepayers is disadvantaged, or improperly subsidized.



         3
             Code of Federal Regulations, Title 18, Chapter 1, Subchapter C, Part 101.

                                             Page 5
                               Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews
                                NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1       If one generation of ratepayers is charged too much depreciation expense,

 2       then a subsequent generation must pay too little, and vice versa.             A

 3       depreciation rate calculated with the proper average service life promotes

 4       intergenerational equity by ensuring that both current and future ratepayers

 5       are responsible for their appropriate share of the utility property that

 6       provides them with utility service.



 7   Q   WHY IS THE ORIGINAL COST OF THE ASSET ADJUSTED FOR

 8       NET SALVAGE?

 9   A   In addition to capital recovery, depreciation rates also contain a provision

10       for net salvage. Net salvage is simply the scrap or reuse value of the asset

11       less the removal cost of the asset being depreciated. Net salvage can be

12       either positive or negative. If the salvage value exceeds the cost of removal,

13       the net salvage is positive. If the cost of removal is greater than the salvage

14       value received as a result of retirement, the resulting net salvage is negative.

15       Accordingly, a utility will also recover the net salvage costs over the useful

16       life of the asset.




                                            Page 6
                            Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews
                             NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1   Q   HOW ARE DEPRECIATION RATES DETERMINED?

 2   A   Depreciation rates are determined using a depreciation system. There are

 3       three components, each with a number of variations, used to determine a

 4       depreciation system, which is then used to estimate depreciation rates. The

 5       three basic components are methods, grouping procedures, and techniques.

 6       The choice of a depreciation system can significantly affect the resulting

 7       depreciation rates.    Typically, a depreciation study will determine the

 8       depreciation rate applicable to each individual account.



 9   Q   PLEASE FURTHER DESCRIBE THE METHODS THAT ARE

10       USED WITHIN A DEPRECIATION SYSTEM.

11   A   There generally are three types of methods of spreading the depreciation

12       expense over the life of property. These are the Straight Line Method,

13       Accelerated Methods, and Deferred Methods. The Straight Line Method is

14       the method most widely used by utility companies for accounting and

15       ratemaking purposes as it is easy to apply and does not create

16       intergenerational inequities because it spreads an equal portion of the plant

17       cost across each accounting period. Accelerated Methods result in higher

18       depreciation rates earlier in an asset’s life, and lower depreciation rates later.

19       Deferred Methods have increasing rates over an asset’s life.



                                          Page 7
                            Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews
                             NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1   Q   PLEASE DESCRIBE THE GROUPING PROCEDURES THAT ARE

 2       USED WITHIN A DEPRECIATION SYSTEM.

 3   A   In order to determine the depreciation rate of an account, the assets within

 4       the account must be grouped together in some manner. There are four main

 5       grouping procedures used within a depreciation system.           These four

 6       procedures are the individual procedure, the Broad Group (more commonly

 7       known as the Average Life Group (“ALG”)), the Vintage Group, and the

 8       Equal Life Group (“ELG”).

 9               In the ALG Procedure, all units within a particular account or

10       category are assumed to be part of a single group that exhibits the same life

11       and retirement characteristics. This is the most common utilized procedure.

12       The Vintage Group and the ELG Procedure assume that sub-groups within

13       a particular account or category may exhibit unique life characteristics. As

14       an example of the Vintage Group Procedure, it may assume that all poles

15       installed in 1985 have a 50-year life, while all poles installed in 1995 have

16       a 45-year life.

17               With the ELG Procedure, it may assume that all poles expected to

18       have a life of 50 years would have one depreciation rate, while poles

19       expected to attain life spans of only 40 years would have a different




                                         Page 8
                          Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews
                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1       depreciation rate. The overall group depreciation rate would be a composite

 2       of the ELG depreciation rates.



 3   Q   PLEASE FURTHER DESCRIBE THE TECHNIQUES THAT ARE

 4       USED WITHIN A DEPRECIATION SYSTEM.

 5   A   There are two techniques used to calculate depreciation rates: Whole Life

 6       and Remaining Life. The Whole Life Technique spreads the original cost

 7       less net salvage of the account over the average life of the account. This

 8       technique requires that separate amortizations be made to correct for over-

 9       and under-accumulations due to changes in an account’s ASL.

10               The Remaining Life Technique spreads the unrecovered cost less

11       net salvage over the remaining life of the account. The Remaining Life

12       Technique is the most common technique used and it has a self-correcting

13       nature that spreads any over- or under-accumulations over the remaining

14       life.




                                          Page 9
                          Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews
                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1   Q   IN YOUR EXPERIENCE, WHAT DEPRECIATION SYSTEM IS

 2       MOST COMMONLY UTILIZED TO DETERMINE UTILITY

3        DEPRECIATION RATES FOR RATEMAKING PURPOSES?

4    A   The most common depreciation system is one that consists of the Straight

5        Line Method, the ALG Procedure, and the Remaining Life Technique.

6        Essentially, this system results in depreciation rates that ensure estimated

7        future accruals are recovered equally over the remaining lives of the assets.



 8   Q   PLEASE DESCRIBE THE ACTUARIAL LIFE ANALYSIS THAT IS

 9       PERFORMED            TO      EVALUATE           HISTORICAL          ASSET

10       RETIREMENT EXPERIENCE.

11   A   Actuarial life analysis (retirement rate method) is described by the National

12       Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners’ (“NARUC”) Public

13       Utility Depreciation Practices Manual (“NARUC Manual”) as follows:

14              Actuarial analysis is the process of using statistics and
15              probability to describe the retirement history of property. The
16              process may be used as a basis for estimating the probable future
17              life characteristics of a group of property.

18              Actuarial analysis requires information in greater detail than do
19              other life analysis models (e.g., turnover, simulation) and, as a
20              result, may be impractical to implement for certain accounts (see
21              Chapter VII). However, for accounts for which application of
22              actuarial analysis is practical; it is a powerful analytical tool
23              and, therefore, is generally considered the preferred
24              approach.

                                        Page 10
                             Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews
                              NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1                 Actuarial analysis objectively measures how the company has
 2                 retired its investment. The analyst must then judge whether this
 3                 historical view depicts the future life of the property in service.
 4                 The analyst takes into consideration various factors, such as
 5                 changes in technology, services provided, or, capital budgets. 4

 6                 As explained by the NARUC Manual, when the required data exists,

 7         meaning a database that contains the year of installation and the year of

 8         retirements for each vintage of property, actuarial life analysis is the

 9         preferred method of determining the life, and thus, retirement

10         characteristics of a group of property. In this type of life analysis, there are

11         three major steps. The first step is to gather and use available aged data

12         from the Company’s continuing plant records to create an observed life

13         table. The observed life table provides the percent surviving for each age

14         interval of property.

15                 The second step is to conduct a fitting analysis to match the actual

16         survivor data from the observed life table to a standard set of mortality or

17         survivor curves. Typically, the observed life table data is matched to Iowa

18         Curves.    The fitting process is a mathematical fitting process, which

19         minimizes the Sum of Squared Differences (“SSD”) between the actual data

20         and the Iowa Curves.




           4
            NARUC Public Utility Depreciation Practices Manual, 1996 at page 111
     (Emphasis Added).

                                           Page 11
                              Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews
                               NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1                 The third step is to select the best fitting curve while using informed

 2       judgment to determine the curve that best represents the property being

 3       studied. This includes the use of a visual matching process. Although the

 4       mathematical fitting process provides a curve that is theoretically possible,

 5       the visual matching process will allow the trained depreciation professional

 6       to use informed judgment in the determination of the best fitting survivor

 7       curve.



 8   Q   PLEASE PROVIDE FURTHER EXPLANATION OF THE SSD

 9       STATISTICAL MEASUREMENT.

10   A   The Actuarial Life Analysis section of the NARUC Manual describes SSD

11       as follows:

12                 Generally, the goodness of fit criterion is the least sum of
13                 squared deviations. The difference between the observed and
14                 projected data is calculated for each data point in the observed
15                 data. This difference is squared, and the resulting amounts are
16                 summed to provide a single statistic that represents the quality
17                 of the fit between the observed and projected curves.

18                 The difference between the observed and projected data points
19                 is squared for two reasons: (1) the importance of large
20                 differences is increased, and (2) the result is a positive number,
21                 hence the squared differences can be summed to generate a
22                 measure of the total absolute difference between the two curves.
23                 The curves with the least sum of squared deviations are
24                 considered the best fits. 5

         5
             NARUC Public Utility Depreciation Practices Manual, 1996 at pages 124-125.

 1   Q   PLEASE DESCRIBE THE SIMULATED PLANT RECORD (“SPR”)

 2       PROCEDURE.

 3   A   The SPR balances model was first presented in Alexander E. Bauhan’s 1947

 4       paper Life Analysis of Utility Plant for Depreciation Accounting Purposes

 5       by the Simulated Plant Record Method. The NARUC Manual describes the

 6       SPR as follows:

 7                 The Simulated Plant Record (SPR) method is used by utilities
 8                 and commissions to indicate generalized survivor curves that
 9                 best represent the life characteristics of property when the
10                 property records do not contain the age of the property upon
11                 retirement. The selection of curves is based upon the closeness
12                 of the match between actual and simulated annual amounts.

13                 The closeness of the match between annual amounts is measured
14                 by the Conformance Index (CI) or its reciprocal, the Index of
15                 Variation (IV). These measures are based upon the sum of
16                 squared differences between simulated and actual annual
17                 amounts. The highest ranked curves are those with the highest
18                 CIs (or lowest IVs).

19                 The maturity of the account is measured by the Retirement
20                 Experience Index (REI). The higher the REI, the more
21                 assurance that a unique retirement pattern was used in the
22                 simulation. In 1947, Bauhan proposed a scale to rank the REI
23                 and the CI from poor to excellent. 6

24                 The SPR method is a commonly used practice when the proper aged

25       vintage data is not available to analyze for an actuarial life analysis. The

26       SPR Balances model applies the survivor factors from a predetermined



         6
             NARUC Public Utility Depreciation Practices Manual, 1996, Page 92.

                                           Page 13
                            Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews
                             NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


1        Iowa Curve and average service life to the actual annual additions of a

2        property account, which produces an estimation of the year-end balances.

3        Goodness of fit statistics are then calculated to determine which curves

4        produce the best match.

5               These goodness of fit statistics are the Conformance Index (“CI”)

6        and the Retirement Experience Index (“REI”). A good fit in both of these

7        measurements is indicated by values above 50. Over 75 is considered

8        excellent. A CI under 25 is considered a poor fit.



9    Q   PLEASE DESCRIBE THE IOWA SURVIVOR CURVES THAT ARE

10       USED IN ACTUARIAL LIFE ANALYSIS AND SPR ANALYSIS.

11   A   The selection of the survivor curve is one of the most important decisions

12       in conducting a depreciation study.        A survivor curve is a graphical

13       representation of the amount of property existing at each age interval

14       throughout the life of a group of property. From the survivor curve,

15       parameters required to calculate depreciation rates can be determined, such

16       as the average service life of the group of property and the composite

17       remaining life.

18              In this proceeding, as well as the majority of utility regulatory rate

19       case proceedings throughout the United States and Canada, the Iowa Curves



                                         Page 14

                        NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1   are the general survivor curves utilized to describe the mortality

 2   characteristics of a group of property. There are four types of Iowa Curves:

 3   right-moded, left-moded, symmetrical-moded, and origin-moded. Each

 4   type describes where the greatest frequency of retirements occurs relative

 5   to the average service life.

 6          A survivor curve often consists of an average service life and Iowa

 7   Curve type combination. For example, when describing property with a

 8   50-year average service life that has mortality characteristics of the R2 Iowa

 9   Curve, the survivor curve would simply be notated as “50-R2.” I present the
